title: Stochastic attention kernel sensitivity notes
content:
Summary:
This is a working log for a set of experiments exploring stochastic variability in attention kernel performance. We observed non-deterministic latency swings (esp. P95/P99) when switching between FlashAttention, paged attention, and fused-op paths under real workload noise. Goal: characterize sensitivity to random seeds, CUDA context reuse, small timing offsets in prefetch, and micro-batching jitter; propose mitigations (warmup policies, determinism knobs, watchdog sampling).

Motivation / hypotheses:
- H1: Some latency variance is due to allocator/context thrash across concurrent streams rather than kernel math.
- H2: FlashAttention shows higher median throughput but higher tail sensitivity when sequence-length mix is variable and KV cache warming is incomplete.
- H3: Small timing jitter in the batch scheduler (e.g., +-1ms) can flip kernel selection heuristics, causing outlier slow kernels.

Test matrix (short):
- Models: gpt2-medium-ish (12-layer proxy), lla-mini proxy (smaller dense dims)
- Kernels: flashattention, paged-attn, fused-matmul-attn (best-effort fused ops)
- Seq lengths: 64, 256, 1024 (mixed stream: random sample 80/15/5)
- Batch sizes: 1, 4, 16
- Noise knobs: scheduler jitter off/on, random seed (0..9), allocator fragmentation profile (cold/warm), prefetch delay 0/1/3ms
- Metrics captured: median latency, p95, p99, throughput (tokens/s), CUDA SM utilization, L2 bw, occcupancy, per-kernel time breakdown

Repro commands (tracebench harness):
- baseline run (no jitter):
  ./run_tracebench.sh --model proxy-gpt2 --kernel flashattention --seq-mix 64:80,256:15,1024:5 --batch 4 --duration 120 --warmup 20 --seed 0 --collect-cuda 

- jittered scheduler (adds small sleep jitter in batcher):
  ./run_tracebench.sh --model proxy-gpt2 --kernel flashattention --seq-mix 64:80,256:15,1024:5 --batch 4 --duration 120 --warmup 20 --seed 3 --batcher-jitter-ms 1 --collect-cuda

- paged attention comparison:
  ./run_tracebench.sh --model proxy-gpt2 --kernel paged-attn --batch 4 --seq-mix 64:80,256:15,1024:5 --duration 120 --warmup 20 --seed 1 --collect-cuda

- fused-ops path (best-effort):
  ./run_tracebench.sh --model proxy-gpt2 --kernel fused-ops --batch 4 --seq-mix 64:80,256:15,1024:5 --duration 120 --warmup 20 --seed 7 --collect-cuda

Observations (notes from runs):
- Run A (flashattention, seed=0, no jitter): median=18.6ms, p95=34.1ms, p99=56.8ms, throughput=7.9k tok/s. CUDA SM util ~68%, L2 bw peaks at 420GB/s.
- Run B (flashattention, seed=3, batcher-jitter 1ms): median=19.1ms (+2.7%), p95=48.2ms (+41%), p99=112.9ms (+99%). Saw 3 distinct long tails where kernel choice fell back to a slow path.
- Run C (paged-attn, seed=1): median=22.8ms, p95=38.9ms, p99=62.4ms, throughput=6.4k tok/s. Tails lower than jittered Flash in same config.
- Run D (fused-ops, seed=7): median=17.9ms (best median), p95=45.3ms, p99=89.7ms. Some fused microkernels had sporadic increases in runtime when run immediately after a long paged-attn invocation (possible cache/occupancy warmdown effect).

Key incidents logged:
- Incident 1 (2024-11-25): when a large seq=1024 request arrives while many small requests are inflight, the runtime sometimes selects a paged-attn fallback that then triggers increased memory thrash and causes later flash kernels to take 2-3x longer. Pattern: mixed-size queue -> heuristic picks fallback -> memory-slab fragmentation -> flash kernel slower.
- Incident 2 (2024-12-03): small scheduler randomness (emulated jitter 1ms) changed ordering such that prefetches missed by one micro-batch, causing first token of some requests to hit page-in path; these requests contributed heavily to p99.

Profiling artifacts collected (summary):
- nvprof traces for 12 representative windows (attached in linked_artifacts).
- per-request kernel timelines from tracebench: heatmap of kernel durations by relative time slice.
- allocator histograms (cudaMalloc/cudaFree patterns) show spikes correlated with p99 events.

Preliminary analysis / hypotheses validated:
- Allocator and memory-slab fragmentation is a major contributor. When paged-attn runs (or a fallback code path does extra device-side allocation), subsequent flash kernels are starved for fast contiguous allocations leading to atomic/work-queue slowdowns.
- Kernel-choice heuristics are threshold-based and brittle to small timing shifts—small jitter changes whether a request is batched with other similar seq-lengths, which in turn changes kernel selection (flash vs paged).
- Fused ops can be fastest median but have higher statefulness across invocations; they rely on certain kernel-launch patterns that are sensitive to stream re-use and prior kernel footprints.

Mitigations to try (prioritized):
1) Warmup policy: ensure first N requests of a newly-started worker use a deterministic warmup sequence (fixed seeds, forced flash kernel) to pre-allocate slabs and prime L2/KV caches.
2) Soft determinism flag: make batch scheduler optionally disable tiny jitter for customers with tight tail SLOs.
3) Allocator tuning: pre-reserve per-stream arena with larger contiguous slabs for attention kernels, reduce on-demand fragmentation by using pooled device allocations.
4) Kernel-selection hysteresis: when switching kernel paths, require a small stability window (e.g., 10 successive requests) before switching back, to avoid flip-flopping.
5) Lightweight watchdog sampling: if p95 or p99 spikes, capture a microtrace and temporarily route similar requests to paged-attn until stabilized.

Open questions / next experiments:
- What is the cost tradeoff of pre-reserving larger slabs per stream? (memory vs tail reduction)
- Can we reproduce the flip-flop deterministically by controlling only ordering (no random seed), to prove scheduler ordering is the causal factor?
- How often does this behavior appear in dedicated vs hosted environments (differences in co-tenancy)?
- Is there a simple kernel-level patch (e.g., adjust launch params) that reduces fused-op sensitivity?

Immediate next steps (owner assigned):
- Priya: build a small repro that enforces ordering changes only (no allocator changes) to validate scheduling causality. Target by 2024-12-01.
- Liam: prototype per-stream preallocation and run mem-frag regression suite. Target by 2024-12-10.
- Marco: add a scheduler flag to disable jitter and run customer-like mixed workloads. Target by 2024-12-08.

Notes to self (choppy):
- stash nvprof logs under s3://redwood-profiling/attn/stochastic/ (curated windows)
- add more seeds (up to 25) but sample smartly (only keep runs with clear outliers)
- check Git PR 412 — has a new allocator that might interact (linked_artifacts)

This doc is a lab notebook; will iterate as new runs land. If you copy/paste any numbers into slides, mark as "preliminary".
